decks.title: Relations and Functions — Part 1: Cartesian products and relations
goals: Write ordered pairs and decide when two ordered pairs are equal
Form the Cartesian product of two sets and count its elements
Describe a relation from a set A to a set B
Find the domain, codomain and range of a relation
Count the relations from one finite set to another

slides.heading: Relations and Functions, Part 1: Pairs and relations
slides.body_md: A canteen menu pairs every snack with every drink. What does that look like in mathematics?

visual.alt: Table of the six snack and drink combinations in an imagined canteen: Samosa, Vada and Idli each paired with Tea and with Lassi, written as ordered pairs.
visual.caption: Every snack paired with every drink: $3 \times 2 = 6$ ordered pairs.

slides.narration: Welcome to Class Eleven mathematics. Picture a canteen that sells three snacks and two drinks. A combo is one snack together with one drink, and the menu lists every possible combo. Each combo is an ordered pair, and the whole menu is a Cartesian product. In this part you will build products, define relations as pieces of a product, and learn to read off domain and range.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Form the **Cartesian product** $A \times B$ and count it
Define a **relation** as a subset of $A \times B$
slides.narration: Here are your goals. You will learn when two ordered pairs are equal, how to list a Cartesian product and count its elements, and what a relation is. You will then practise finding the domain, codomain and range, and counting how many different relations exist between two small sets. Questions on these appear as one-mark objectives and two or three mark short answers.

slides.heading: Ordered pairs
slides.body_md: An **ordered pair** $(a, b)$ has a first entry and a second entry. $(a, b) = (c, d)$ exactly when $a = c$ **and** $b = d$.

visual.alt: Two points on a grid: (2, 5) is two units across and five up; (5, 2) is five across and two up. They are different points, so the pairs are different.
visual.caption: Order matters: $(2, 5) \ne (5, 2)$.

slides.narration: An ordered pair is two entries written in a fixed order. The pair two comma five is not the same as five comma two, just as the point two across and five up is different from the point five across and two up. Two ordered pairs are equal only when both the first entries match and the second entries match.

slides.heading: The Cartesian product
slides.body_md: $A \times B = \{(a, b) : a \in A,\ b \in B\}$: every element of $A$ paired with every element of $B$, first entry from $A$.

visual.alt: Grid table for A equal to 1, 2, 3 and B equal to x, y: each row is an element of A, each column an element of B, and each cell is the ordered pair (row, column), six cells in all.
visual.caption: $A \times B$ for $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$ and $B = \{x, y\}$: six cells, six pairs.

math: A \times B = \{(a, b) : a \in A,\ b \in B\}
slides.narration: The Cartesian product of A and B is the set of all ordered pairs whose first entry comes from A and whose second entry comes from B. A grid table helps: put the elements of A down the side, the elements of B across the top, and each cell is one pair. With three rows and two columns there are six pairs.

slides.heading: A product as points on a grid
slides.body_md: Plotted, $\{1, 2, 3\} \times \{4, 5\}$ is a rectangular lattice of points.

visual.alt: Six points on a grid for A equal to 1, 2, 3 and B equal to 4, 5: three columns at x equal to 1, 2, 3 and two rows at y equal to 4 and 5, forming a rectangle of lattice points.
visual.caption: The product $\{1, 2, 3\} \times \{4, 5\}$ plotted as points: a $3$ by $2$ lattice.

slides.narration: When the sets contain numbers, each ordered pair is a point in the plane. Here the first set is one, two, three and the second is four, five. The six pairs form a neat lattice with three columns and two rows. Notice that the real plane itself is the Cartesian product of the real line with itself.

slides.heading: A × B and B × A are different
slides.body_md: $A \times B = B \times A$ only when $A = B$ (or one set is empty). Otherwise the products have the **same size** but **different elements**.

visual.alt: Table comparing A cross B and B cross A for A equal to 1, 2 and B equal to 3, 4. Each has four pairs, but the lists are different and have no pair in common.
visual.caption: $A = \{1, 2\}$, $B = \{3, 4\}$: same size, different sets.

slides.narration: Because order matters, A cross B and B cross A are usually different sets. For A equal to one, two and B equal to three, four, both products have four pairs, but they share no pair at all. The first list has pairs like one comma three; the second has three comma one. Same size, different elements. Always keep the order of the sets straight.

slides.heading: Counting a product
slides.body_md: If $n(A) = p$ and $n(B) = q$, then $n(A \times B) = pq$. In particular $n(A \times A) = p^2$.

visual.alt: Table of counts: with n(A) and n(B) equal to 2 and 3 there are 6 pairs in A cross B and 4 in A cross A; 3 and 4 give 12 and 9; 5 and 5 give 25 and 25; 1 and 6 give 6 and 1.
visual.caption: $n(A \times B) = n(A) \times n(B)$.

slides.narration: Each of the p elements of the first set pairs with each of the q elements of the second, so the product has p times q elements. The table was made by listing the pairs. When the two sets are the same, the product has p squared elements. If either set is empty, the product is empty.

slides.heading: Quick check: size of a product
slides.body_md: A set has four elements and another has five. How large is the Cartesian product?
slides.narration: Multiply the two sizes. Do not add them.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: products and equal pairs
slides.body_md: $A = \{2, 3\}$ and $B = \{1, 4, 5\}$. List $A \times B$, $B \times A$ and $A \times A$. Then find $x$ and $y$ if $(x + 1,\ 2y - 3) = (4,\ 7)$.
bullets: **Lists —** as in the table: first entry from the first set

visual.alt: Table of three products for A equal to 2, 3 and B equal to 1, 4, 5: A cross B has six pairs, B cross A has six pairs, and A cross A has four pairs.
visual.caption: $A = \{2, 3\}$, $B = \{1, 4, 5\}$.

slides.narration: List each product by taking every first entry with every second entry. A cross B and B cross A each have six pairs and A cross A has four. For the equation, equal ordered pairs have equal entries in matching positions. So x plus one equals four gives x equal to three, and two y minus three equals seven gives y equal to five.

slides.heading: What is a relation?
slides.body_md: A **relation** $R$ from $A$ to $B$ is any **subset** of $A \times B$. We write $x\,R\,y$ when $(x, y) \in R$.

visual.alt: Arrow diagram of a relation from A equal to 1, 2, 3, 4 to B equal to 1, 3, 5, 7, 9: 1 points to 1, 2 to 3, 3 to 5 and 4 to 7. The element 9 of B receives no arrow.
visual.caption: $R = \{(x, y) : y = 2x - 1\}$ from $A$ to $B$.

slides.narration: A relation from A to B picks out some of the pairs of the product. It can be a few pairs, all of them, or none. In the arrow diagram, each arrow is one pair. Here the rule is y equals two x minus one: one goes to one, two goes to three, three goes to five, and four goes to seven. The element nine in the second set receives no arrow.

slides.heading: Domain, codomain and range
slides.body_md: **Domain:** all first entries. **Codomain:** the whole set $B$. **Range:** the second entries that actually occur, so range $\subseteq$ codomain.

visual.alt: Table of the domain, codomain and range of the relation y equals 2 x minus 1 from A to B: the domain is 1, 2, 3, 4; the codomain is 1, 3, 5, 7, 9; the range is 1, 3, 5, 7.
visual.caption: The range is a subset of the codomain: $9$ is never used.

slides.narration: Three sets describe a relation. The domain is the set of first entries. The codomain is the whole target set B, whether or not every element is used. The range is the set of second entries that really occur, so it can be smaller than the codomain. In our relation the range is one, three, five, seven, and nine is left out.

slides.heading: Four ways to describe a relation
slides.body_md: The same relation can be given as a **roster**, a **rule**, an **arrow diagram** or a **table**. Be ready to switch between them.

rows: one arrow for each pair (see the previous slide)

visual.alt: Table of four ways to describe the same relation: listing its pairs, a rule in set-builder form, an arrow diagram, or a table of x and y values.
visual.caption: One relation, four descriptions.

slides.narration: Questions give a relation in different forms. You can list the pairs, which is the roster form. You can state a rule in set-builder form. You can draw arrows between two boxes. Or you can tabulate the first and second entries side by side. Practise moving between these forms, because converting to a list of pairs makes the domain and range easy to read.

slides.heading: Quick check: pairs of a relation
slides.body_md: How many ordered pairs does the relation x less than y have, from {1, 2, 3} to {2, 3, 4}?
slides.narration: Go through each first entry and count the second entries that are larger.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: from a rule to a list

visual.alt: Table of y equal to x squared minus 3 x for x from 0 to 4: the values are 0, minus 2, minus 2, 0 and 4. Each is in B, so each x gives a pair of R.
visual.caption: The range is $\{-2, 0, 4\}$.

slides.narration: Substitute each element of A into the rule and check that the answer lies in B. The values are zero, minus two, minus two, zero and four, all inside B. So the relation has five pairs. Every element of A is a first entry, so the domain is all of A. The second entries, written once each, give the range: minus two, zero and four.

slides.heading: Counting relations
slides.body_md: $A \times B$ has $pq$ pairs and a relation is any subset of it, so there are $2^{pq}$ relations from $A$ to $B$.

visual.alt: Table counting relations by listing them: with 1 and 1 elements there are 2 relations; 1 and 2 give 4; 2 and 2 give 16; 2 and 3 give 64. The number of pairs is p times q and the number of relations is 2 to the power p q.
visual.caption: Counts checked by listing every subset of $A \times B$.

math: \text{number of relations from } A \text{ to } B = 2^{pq}
slides.narration: To build a relation, decide for each pair of the product whether it is in or out. With p times q pairs, that is two choices each, giving two to the power p q relations. The table was built by listing every subset. From a set of two to a set of three elements there are sixty-four relations. Remember to count subsets, not pairs.

slides.heading: Quick check: a false claim
slides.body_md: True or false: for two different non-empty sets, A cross B equals B cross A.
slides.narration: Try the smallest case: one set holds the number one and the other holds the number two.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: reading an arrow diagram
slides.body_md: The diagram shows a relation from $X = \{a, b, c, d\}$ to $Y = \{1, 2, 3\}$. Write the pairs, the domain and the range.
bullets: **Domain —** $\{a, b, d\}$: the element $c$ has no arrow, so it is **not** in the domain

visual.alt: Arrow diagram of a relation from X equal to a, b, c, d to Y equal to 1, 2, 3: a points to 1 and 2, b to 2, d to 3. The element c has no arrow.
visual.caption: The element $c$ has no arrow: it is not in the domain.

slides.narration: Read each arrow as a pair. A has two arrows, to one and to two. B has one arrow to two. D has one arrow to three. C has no arrow. The domain is only the set of first entries that appear, so it is A, B, D, and C is left out. The range is one, two, three. Notice that the domain can be smaller than the first set.

slides.heading: Quick check: count a product
slides.body_md: Count the elements of the product of the primes below twelve and the multiples of three between zero and twenty.
slides.narration: Write out each set first, count them, then multiply.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Ordered pairs: $(a, b) = (c, d)$ iff $a = c$ and $b = d$
$A \times B$: all pairs $(a, b)$; $n(A \times B) = pq$
Relation from $A$ to $B$: a subset of $A \times B$; $2^{pq}$ of them
Domain = first entries; codomain = $B$; range = second entries used

visual.alt: Summary flow: ordered pairs build the Cartesian product A cross B; a relation is a subset of A cross B; each relation has a domain, a codomain and a range.
visual.caption: From pairs to relations.

slides.narration: To sum up. Ordered pairs have a fixed order. The Cartesian product collects all pairs, and it has p times q elements. A relation is any subset of the product, and there are two to the power p q of them. For each relation, the domain holds the first entries, the codomain is the whole second set, and the range holds the second entries that occur.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Product listing (1–2 marks):** correct pairs, correct order, correct count
**Relation from a rule (2–3 marks):** roster form 1, domain and range 1–2
**Equal ordered pairs (1–2 marks):** compare entries position by position
**Mistake:** writing $B \times A$ when $A \times B$ is asked
**Mistake:** giving the codomain as the range
slides.narration: For product questions, marks go for the right pairs in the right order and the right count. For relations given by a rule, write the roster form first, then read off the domain and the range. Watch three common slips: reversing the order of the product, giving the whole codomain as the range, and counting the pairs instead of the subsets when asked for the number of relations.

decks.title: Relations and Functions — Part 2: Functions and their graphs
goals: Decide whether a relation is a function, and find domain and range
Recognise and sketch the standard real functions
Evaluate functions such as the signum and greatest integer functions
Add, subtract, multiply and divide real functions with their domains

slides.heading: Relations and Functions, Part 2: Functions
slides.body_md: A function is a rule that gives exactly one output for every allowed input.

visual.alt: Flow diagram of a function as a machine: an input x goes into a rule that adds three and then doubles, and exactly one output f of x comes out.
visual.caption: A function: one output for each allowed input.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Think of a function as a machine. You put in an input, the machine applies a fixed rule, and exactly one output comes out. In this part you will meet functions as a special kind of relation, learn how to find their domain and range, study the graphs of the standard real functions, and learn to combine functions by adding, multiplying and dividing them.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Tell a **function** from a relation that is not one
Know the graphs of **constant, identity, polynomial, rational, modulus, signum** and **greatest integer** functions
Use $f + g$, $f - g$, $fg$, $f/g$ with their domains
slides.narration: Here are your goals for part two. You will recognise functions, find their domains and ranges, and know the shapes of the standard graphs. You will also do algebra with functions and find the domain of each combination. Composition of functions is included here for your own understanding; the board does not assess it in the annual paper.

slides.heading: A function is a special relation
slides.body_md: A relation $f$ from $A$ to $B$ is a **function** if **every** $x \in A$ has **exactly one** image $f(x) \in B$. So the domain is all of $A$.

visual.alt: Arrow diagram of the squaring function from A equal to minus 2, minus 1, 1, 2 to B equal to 1, 4, 9: minus 2 and 2 go to 4, minus 1 and 1 go to 1. The element 9 of B receives no arrow.
visual.caption: $f(x) = x^2$: one arrow from every element of $A$; range $\{1, 4\}$.

slides.narration: A function is a relation in which every element of the domain has exactly one arrow leaving it. Two different inputs may share an output, as minus two and two both go to four here. The codomain may have unused elements, like nine. The range is the set of outputs actually used. For the squaring function on this set, the range is one and four.

slides.heading: When a relation is not a function
slides.body_md: Two failures: an input with **two** images, or an input with **none**.

visual.alt: Arrow diagram of a relation that is not a function: the element 1 has two arrows, to a and to b, and the element 3 has no arrow at all.
visual.caption: Not a function: $1$ has two images and $3$ has none.

slides.narration: There are two ways for a relation to fail the test. In this diagram the element one has two arrows, so it has two different images, which is not allowed. The element three has no arrow at all, so it has no image, which is also not allowed. Notice that the element two is fine: one arrow only.

slides.heading: The vertical line test
slides.body_md: If a vertical line meets a graph at **two** points, the graph is **not** the graph of a function of $x$.

visual.alt: The sideways parabola x equal to y squared drawn as an upper branch y equal to square root of x and a lower branch y equal to minus square root of x. The vertical line x equal to 4 meets it at the two points (4, 2) and (4, minus 2).
visual.caption: A vertical line meets $x = y^2$ twice: not a function of $x$.

slides.narration: For graphs, there is a quick test. Draw a vertical line. If it ever meets the graph in two points, then one input has two outputs, and the graph is not a function of x. The sideways parabola x equals y squared fails: the line x equals four meets it at the points four comma two and four comma minus two.

slides.heading: Domain and range of a real function
slides.body_md: **Domain:** every real $x$ for which the rule makes sense (no division by zero, no square root of a negative). **Range:** solve $y = f(x)$ for $x$ and see which $y$ are possible.

visual.alt: Table of three real functions with their domains and ranges: square root of x minus 2 has domain from 2 up and range from 0 up; 1 over x minus 3 has domain all reals except 3 and range all reals except 0; square root of 9 minus x squared has domain minus 3 to 3 and range 0 to 3.
visual.caption: Domain from where the rule works; range by solving $y = f(x)$ for $x$.

slides.narration: For a real function, the domain is every real number for which the rule works. Watch for denominators that are zero and square roots of negative numbers. To find the range, write y equals f of x, solve for x, and see which values of y allow a real solution. The table shows three examples, each checked by testing many values.

slides.heading: Constant and identity functions
slides.body_md: **Constant:** $f(x) = c$, range $\{c\}$. **Identity:** $f(x) = x$, range $\mathbb{R}$. Both have domain $\mathbb{R}$.

visual.alt: A horizontal line y equals 3, the constant function, and the diagonal line y equals x, the identity function. They meet at (3, 3). The diagonal passes through the origin and the point (minus 2, minus 2).
visual.caption: Constant: range $\{3\}$. Identity: range $\mathbb{R}$.

slides.narration: The constant function gives the same output, here three, for every input, so its graph is a horizontal line and its range has just one element. The identity function returns its input unchanged, so its graph is the diagonal line, and the range is all real numbers. Here the two lines meet at the point three comma three.

slides.heading: Polynomial functions
slides.body_md: $f(x) = a_0 + a_1 x + \cdots + a_n x^n$ has domain $\mathbb{R}$. $x^2$ has range $[0, \infty)$; $x^3$ has range $\mathbb{R}$.

visual.alt: Two polynomial graphs: the U-shaped parabola y equal x squared and the S-shaped cubic y equal x cubed. Both pass through (0, 0) and (1, 1); the parabola passes through (2, 4) and the cubic through (minus 2, minus 8).
visual.caption: $x^2$ has range $[0, \infty)$; $x^3$ has range $\mathbb{R}$.

slides.narration: A polynomial function is built from powers of x, so it works for every real input. The square function makes a U shape and never goes below zero, so its range is zero upward. The cube function rises from the lower left to the upper right, taking every real value, so its range is all real numbers. Both pass through the origin and the point one comma one.

slides.heading: Rational functions
slides.body_md: $f(x) = \dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}$ is defined where $q(x) \ne 0$. For $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}$: domain $\mathbb{R} - \{0\}$, range $\mathbb{R} - \{0\}$.

visual.alt: The graph of y equal 1 over x in two separate branches: one in the first quadrant through (1, 1) and (2, 0.5), one in the third quadrant through (minus 1, minus 1) and (minus 2, minus 0.5). There is no point on the vertical axis.
visual.caption: Domain $\mathbb{R} - \{0\}$, range $\mathbb{R} - \{0\}$.

slides.narration: A rational function is a fraction of two polynomials, and it is undefined wherever the denominator is zero. The reciprocal function one over x has two branches, one for positive x and one for negative x, with nothing at x equal to zero. It never takes the value zero either, so both its domain and its range are all real numbers except zero.

slides.heading: Quick check: domain of a rational function
slides.body_md: Find the domain of the function x plus one over x squared minus four.
slides.narration: Which values of x make the denominator zero?

slides.heading: The modulus function
slides.body_md: $|x| = x$ for $x \ge 0$ and $-x$ for $x < 0$. Domain $\mathbb{R}$, range $[0, \infty)$.

visual.alt: The V-shaped graph of y equals the modulus of x, with its corner at the origin and passing through (minus 3, 3) and (3, 3). It never goes below the x-axis.
visual.caption: The modulus function: domain $\mathbb{R}$, range $[0, \infty)$.

slides.narration: The modulus function returns the distance of a number from zero. For zero and positive numbers it leaves them alone; for negative numbers it flips the sign. Its graph is a V with the corner at the origin. The domain is all real numbers, and because distances are never negative, the range is zero and upward.

slides.heading: The signum function
slides.body_md: $\operatorname{sgn}(x) = 1$ if $x > 0$, $0$ if $x = 0$, $-1$ if $x < 0$. Range $\{-1, 0, 1\}$.

visual.alt: The signum function: a flat line at height minus 1 for negative x, a single point at the origin where the value is 0, and a flat line at height 1 for positive x.
visual.caption: Signum: range $\{-1, 0, 1\}$.

slides.narration: The signum function reports only the sign of a number. It gives one for positive numbers, minus one for negative numbers, and zero at zero. Its graph is two flat half-lines with a single point at the origin. The range has just three elements: minus one, zero and one. The domain is all the real numbers.

slides.heading: The greatest integer function
slides.body_md: $[x]$ is the greatest integer **not exceeding** $x$. E.g. $[2.9] = 2$, $[-0.4] = -1$. Domain $\mathbb{R}$, range $\mathbb{Z}$.

visual.alt: The greatest integer function drawn as a staircase of flat steps from x equal to minus 2 up to 4: each step has height equal to its left end, with marked points (minus 2, minus 2), (minus 1, minus 1), (1, 1), (2, 2) and (3, 3).
visual.caption: A staircase: $[x]$ jumps by $1$ at every integer.

slides.narration: The greatest integer function rounds a number down to the nearest integer at or below it. So two point nine becomes two, and minus zero point four becomes minus one, not zero. Its graph is a staircase: flat between consecutive integers, jumping up by one at each integer. The domain is all real numbers, and the range is the set of all integers.

slides.heading: Quick check: floor and signum
slides.body_md: Evaluate the greatest integer of minus two point three, minus the signum of minus four, plus the greatest integer of one point eight.
slides.narration: Find each value separately, and be careful with the minus sign.

slides.heading: Exponential and logarithmic functions
slides.body_md: $2^x$: domain $\mathbb{R}$, range $(0, \infty)$. $\log_2 x$: domain $(0, \infty)$, range $\mathbb{R}$. Their graphs mirror each other in $y = x$.

visual.alt: Two curves: the rising exponential y equal 2 to the power x through (0, 1), (1, 2) and (2, 4), and the logarithm y equal log base 2 of x through (1, 0), (2, 1) and (4, 2). They are mirror images in the line y equal x.
visual.caption: Exponential: domain $\mathbb{R}$, range $(0, \infty)$. Logarithm: domain $(0, \infty)$, range $\mathbb{R}$.

slides.narration: Two more graphs appear in the syllabus. The exponential function two to the power x is defined for every real x and is always positive. The logarithm to base two is defined only for positive x and takes every real value. Their graphs are mirror images in the line y equals x. You only need to recognise their shapes and their domains and ranges here.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: domain and range of a root
slides.body_md: Find the domain and range of $f(x) = \sqrt{9 - x^2}$.

visual.alt: The upper half of a circle of radius 3 centred at the origin: the graph of y equals the square root of 9 minus x squared, from x equal to minus 3 to x equal to 3, rising to a top at (0, 3). Marked points include (1.8, 2.4).
visual.caption: Domain $[-3, 3]$, range $[0, 3]$.

slides.narration: The square root needs a non-negative number inside, so nine minus x squared must be at least zero. That means x lies between minus three and three. Inside this interval the expression ranges from zero up to nine, so the square root ranges from zero up to three. Every value from zero to three is reached. The graph is the upper half of a circle of radius three.

slides.heading: Quick check: is it a function?
slides.body_md: Which of these relations from {1, 2, 3} to {a, b} is a function?
slides.narration: Every element of the first set needs exactly one arrow.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a modulus graph
slides.body_md: Sketch $f(x) = |x - 2| + 1$ and find its range.
bullets: **Shift —** the graph of $|x|$ moved $2$ units right and $1$ unit up

visual.alt: The V-shaped graph of y equals the modulus of x minus 2, plus 1. Its lowest point is (2, 1); it passes through (1, 2) and (3, 2) on either side, and through (0, 3) and (4, 3). The graph never touches the x-axis.
visual.caption: Vertex $(2, 1)$; range $[1, \infty)$.

slides.narration: Start from the V-shaped graph of the modulus function. Subtracting two inside the modulus shifts it two units to the right, and adding one outside shifts it one unit up. The corner moves from the origin to two comma one, which is the lowest point. Since the modulus is never negative, the function never goes below one. The range is one and upward.

slides.heading: Algebra of real functions
slides.body_md: On the **common domain** $D_f \cap D_g$: $(f \pm g)(x) = f(x) \pm g(x)$, $(fg)(x) = f(x)g(x)$. For $\dfrac{f}{g}$ also remove the $x$ with $g(x) = 0$.

visual.alt: Table of the four combinations of f of x equal square root of x and g of x equal x minus 4: the sum, difference and product have domain from 0 up, the quotient also excludes 4; at x equal 9 the values are 8, minus 2, 15 and three fifths.
visual.caption: $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ and $g(x) = x - 4$.

slides.narration: Two real functions can be added, subtracted and multiplied wherever both are defined, that is, on the intersection of their domains. For a quotient you must also remove every point where the divisor is zero. The table uses the square root function and x minus four. At x equal nine, the sum is eight, the difference minus two, the product fifteen, and the quotient three fifths.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: domains and values
slides.body_md: $f(x) = \sqrt{x - 1}$ and $g(x) = x - 5$. Find the domains of $f + g$ and $\dfrac{f}{g}$, and the values of $(fg)(10)$ and $\left(\dfrac{f}{g}\right)(10)$.

visual.alt: Table for f of x equal square root of x minus 1 and g of x equal x minus 5: the sum and product have domain from 1 up, the quotient also excludes 5; at x equal 10 the product is 15 and the quotient is three fifths.
visual.caption: $f(x) = \sqrt{x - 1}$, $g(x) = x - 5$.

slides.narration: First find the domain of each function: the root needs x at least one, and the linear function works everywhere. The sum lives on the common domain, one and upward. The quotient must also avoid x equal to five, where the divisor vanishes. At x equal ten the root gives three and the linear function gives five, so the product is fifteen and the quotient is three fifths.

slides.heading: Quick check: product of functions

sections.heading: 1. Ordered pairs and the Cartesian product
sections.body_md:
An **ordered pair** $(a, b)$ has a first and a second entry. $(a, b) = (c, d)$ exactly when $a = c$ and $b = d$.

The **Cartesian product** $A \times B = \{(a, b) : a \in A,\ b \in B\}$.

- $A \times B \ne B \times A$ in general (equal only if $A = B$ or one is empty).
- If $A$ or $B$ is empty, so is $A \times B$.
- $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ is the coordinate plane.

List a product with a grid table: elements of $A$ down the side, of $B$ across the top, each cell a pair.

key_terms.definition_md: Two entries in a fixed order.
All ordered pairs with first entry from $A$ and second from $B$.

formulas.latex: (a, b) = (c, d) \iff a = c \text{ and } b = d
formulas.label: Equal ordered pairs

visual.alt: Grid table for A equal to 1, 2, 3 and B equal to x, y: each row is an element of A, each column an element of B, and each cell is the ordered pair (row, column), six cells in all.
visual.caption: $A \times B$ for $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$ and $B = \{x, y\}$: six cells, six pairs.

visuals.alt: Two points on a grid: (2, 5) is two units across and five up; (5, 2) is five across and two up. They are different points, so the pairs are different.
visuals.caption: Order matters: $(2, 5) \ne (5, 2)$.

sections.heading: 2. Counting a Cartesian product
sections.body_md:
If $n(A) = p$ and $n(B) = q$ then $n(A \times B) = pq$ and $n(A \times A) = p^2$.

The products $A \times B$ and $B \times A$ have the **same size** but, for $A \ne B$, **different elements**.

Plotted on a grid, a product of two sets of numbers is a lattice of points; the pair $(a, b)$ is the point $a$ across and $b$ up.

key_terms.definition_md: The number of elements of the product: $n(A)\,n(B)$.

visual.alt: Table of counts: with n(A) and n(B) equal to 2 and 3 there are 6 pairs in A cross B and 4 in A cross A; 3 and 4 give 12 and 9; 5 and 5 give 25 and 25; 1 and 6 give 6 and 1.
visual.caption: $n(A \times B) = n(A) \times n(B)$.

visuals.alt: Six points on a grid for A equal to 1, 2, 3 and B equal to 4, 5: three columns at x equal to 1, 2, 3 and two rows at y equal to 4 and 5, forming a rectangle of lattice points.
visuals.caption: The product $\{1, 2, 3\} \times \{4, 5\}$ plotted as points: a $3$ by $2$ lattice.

visuals.alt: Table comparing A cross B and B cross A for A equal to 1, 2 and B equal to 3, 4. Each has four pairs, but the lists are different and have no pair in common.
visuals.caption: $A = \{1, 2\}$, $B = \{3, 4\}$: same size, different sets.

sections.heading: 3. Relations
sections.body_md:
A **relation** from $A$ to $B$ is any subset of $A \times B$; $x\,R\,y$ means $(x, y) \in R$. A relation on $A$ is a subset of $A \times A$.

A relation can be described by a **roster** (list of pairs), a **rule** (set-builder), an **arrow diagram** or a **table**. Convert to a list of pairs first: everything else is then easy to read.

Example: $y = x^2 - 3x$ on $\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$ gives $\{(0, 0), (1, -2), (2, -2), (3, 0), (4, 4)\}$.

key_terms.definition_md: Listing the ordered pairs one by one.

visual.alt: Arrow diagram of a relation from A equal to 1, 2, 3, 4 to B equal to 1, 3, 5, 7, 9: 1 points to 1, 2 to 3, 3 to 5 and 4 to 7. The element 9 of B receives no arrow.
visual.caption: $R = \{(x, y) : y = 2x - 1\}$ from $A$ to $B$.

rows: one arrow for each pair (see the previous slide)

visuals.alt: Table of four ways to describe the same relation: listing its pairs, a rule in set-builder form, an arrow diagram, or a table of x and y values.
visuals.caption: One relation, four descriptions.

visuals.alt: Table of y equal to x squared minus 3 x for x from 0 to 4: the values are 0, minus 2, minus 2, 0 and 4. Each is in B, so each x gives a pair of R.
visuals.caption: The range is $\{-2, 0, 4\}$.

sections.heading: 4. Domain, codomain and range
sections.body_md:
For a relation $R$ from $A$ to $B$:

- **Domain** = set of all first entries (a subset of $A$).
- **Codomain** = the whole set $B$.
- **Range** = set of second entries that occur (a subset of $B$).

Elements of $A$ with no arrow are **not** in the domain; elements of $B$ with no arrow are in the codomain but not in the range.

Number of relations from $A$ to $B$: $2^{pq}$ (each of the $pq$ pairs is in or out). Non-empty relations: $2^{pq} - 1$.

visual.alt: Table of the domain, codomain and range of the relation y equals 2 x minus 1 from A to B: the domain is 1, 2, 3, 4; the codomain is 1, 3, 5, 7, 9; the range is 1, 3, 5, 7.
visual.caption: The range is a subset of the codomain: $9$ is never used.

visuals.alt: Table counting relations by listing them: with 1 and 1 elements there are 2 relations; 1 and 2 give 4; 2 and 2 give 16; 2 and 3 give 64. The number of pairs is p times q and the number of relations is 2 to the power p q.
visuals.caption: Counts checked by listing every subset of $A \times B$.

visuals.alt: Arrow diagram of a relation from X equal to a, b, c, d to Y equal to 1, 2, 3: a points to 1 and 2, b to 2, d to 3. The element c has no arrow.
visuals.caption: The element $c$ has no arrow: it is not in the domain.

sections.heading: 5. Functions
sections.body_md:
A relation $f$ from $A$ to $B$ is a **function** if every $x \in A$ has **exactly one** image $f(x) \in B$. Then the domain is $A$, the codomain is $B$ and the range is $\{f(x) : x \in A\} \subseteq B$.

Failures: an element with **two** arrows or with **none**. Two different inputs may share an output.

**Vertical line test:** a graph is a function of $x$ if every vertical line meets it at most once.

Between finite sets with $p$ and $q$ elements there are $q^p$ functions among the $2^{pq}$ relations.

key_terms.definition_md: A relation giving every element of the domain exactly one image.

visual.alt: Arrow diagram of the squaring function from A equal to minus 2, minus 1, 1, 2 to B equal to 1, 4, 9: minus 2 and 2 go to 4, minus 1 and 1 go to 1. The element 9 of B receives no arrow.
visual.caption: $f(x) = x^2$: one arrow from every element of $A$; range $\{1, 4\}$.

visuals.alt: Arrow diagram of a relation that is not a function: the element 1 has two arrows, to a and to b, and the element 3 has no arrow at all.
visuals.caption: Not a function: $1$ has two images and $3$ has none.

visuals.alt: The sideways parabola x equal to y squared drawn as an upper branch y equal to square root of x and a lower branch y equal to minus square root of x. The vertical line x equal to 4 meets it at the two points (4, 2) and (4, minus 2).
visuals.caption: A vertical line meets $x = y^2$ twice: not a function of $x$.

sections.heading: 6. Domain and range of real functions
sections.body_md:
A **real function** has domain and range inside $\mathbb{R}$. **Domain:** all real $x$ where the rule works: no zero denominator, no root of a negative, $x > 0$ for a logarithm.

**Range:** write $y = f(x)$, solve for $x$ in terms of $y$, and keep the $y$ for which a real $x$ in the domain exists.

Examples: $\sqrt{x - 2}$: domain $[2, \infty)$, range $[0, \infty)$. $\dfrac{1}{x - 3}$: domain and range both $\mathbb{R}$ minus one point. $\sqrt{9 - x^2}$: domain $[-3, 3]$, range $[0, 3]$.

Two functions are **equal** only when their domains and rules both agree.

key_terms.definition_md: A function whose domain and range are sets of real numbers.

formulas.latex: y = f(x) \;\Rightarrow\; x = \dots \text{ in terms of } y
formulas.label: Finding the range

visual.alt: Table of three real functions with their domains and ranges: square root of x minus 2 has domain from 2 up and range from 0 up; 1 over x minus 3 has domain all reals except 3 and range all reals except 0; square root of 9 minus x squared has domain minus 3 to 3 and range 0 to 3.
visual.caption: Domain from where the rule works; range by solving $y = f(x)$ for $x$.

visuals.alt: The upper half of a circle of radius 3 centred at the origin: the graph of y equals the square root of 9 minus x squared, from x equal to minus 3 to x equal to 3, rising to a top at (0, 3). Marked points include (1.8, 2.4).
visuals.caption: Domain $[-3, 3]$, range $[0, 3]$.

sections.heading: 7. Standard real functions and their graphs
sections.body_md:
- **Constant** $f(x) = c$: horizontal line, range $\{c\}$. **Identity** $f(x) = x$: range $\mathbb{R}$.
- **Polynomial:** domain $\mathbb{R}$; $x^2$ has range $[0, \infty)$, $x^3$ has range $\mathbb{R}$.
- **Rational** $\dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}$: domain excludes $q(x) = 0$; $\dfrac{1}{x}$ has domain and range $\mathbb{R} - \{0\}$.
- **Modulus** $|x|$: V-shaped, range $[0, \infty)$. $|x - a| + b$ has its corner at $(a, b)$.
- **Signum:** $1, 0, -1$; range $\{-1, 0, 1\}$.
- **Greatest integer** $[x]$: staircase, range $\mathbb{Z}$. $[2.9] = 2$, $[-0.4] = -1$.
- **Exponential** $2^x$: range $(0, \infty)$. **Logarithm** $\log_2 x$: domain $(0, \infty)$, range $\mathbb{R}$; mirror images in $y = x$.

key_terms.definition_md: $1, 0$ or $-1$ according to the sign of $x$.

visual.alt: The V-shaped graph of y equals the modulus of x, with its corner at the origin and passing through (minus 3, 3) and (3, 3). It never goes below the x-axis.
visual.caption: The modulus function: domain $\mathbb{R}$, range $[0, \infty)$.

visuals.alt: A horizontal line y equals 3, the constant function, and the diagonal line y equals x, the identity function. They meet at (3, 3). The diagonal passes through the origin and the point (minus 2, minus 2).
visuals.caption: Constant: range $\{3\}$. Identity: range $\mathbb{R}$.

visuals.alt: Two polynomial graphs: the U-shaped parabola y equal x squared and the S-shaped cubic y equal x cubed. Both pass through (0, 0) and (1, 1); the parabola passes through (2, 4) and the cubic through (minus 2, minus 8).
visuals.caption: $x^2$ has range $[0, \infty)$; $x^3$ has range $\mathbb{R}$.

visuals.alt: The graph of y equal 1 over x in two separate branches: one in the first quadrant through (1, 1) and (2, 0.5), one in the third quadrant through (minus 1, minus 1) and (minus 2, minus 0.5). There is no point on the vertical axis.
visuals.caption: Domain $\mathbb{R} - \{0\}$, range $\mathbb{R} - \{0\}$.

visuals.alt: The signum function: a flat line at height minus 1 for negative x, a single point at the origin where the value is 0, and a flat line at height 1 for positive x.
visuals.caption: Signum: range $\{-1, 0, 1\}$.

visuals.alt: The greatest integer function drawn as a staircase of flat steps from x equal to minus 2 up to 4: each step has height equal to its left end, with marked points (minus 2, minus 2), (minus 1, minus 1), (1, 1), (2, 2) and (3, 3).
visuals.caption: A staircase: $[x]$ jumps by $1$ at every integer.

visuals.alt: Two curves: the rising exponential y equal 2 to the power x through (0, 1), (1, 2) and (2, 4), and the logarithm y equal log base 2 of x through (1, 0), (2, 1) and (4, 2). They are mirror images in the line y equal x.
visuals.caption: Exponential: domain $\mathbb{R}$, range $(0, \infty)$. Logarithm: domain $(0, \infty)$, range $\mathbb{R}$.

visuals.alt: The V-shaped graph of y equals the modulus of x minus 2, plus 1. Its lowest point is (2, 1); it passes through (1, 2) and (3, 2) on either side, and through (0, 3) and (4, 3). The graph never touches the x-axis.
visuals.caption: Vertex $(2, 1)$; range $[1, \infty)$.

sections.heading: 8. Algebra of real functions and composition
sections.body_md:
On the common domain $D_f \cap D_g$:

- $(f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)$ and $(f - g)(x) = f(x) - g(x)$.
- $(fg)(x) = f(x)\,g(x)$ and $(cf)(x) = c\,f(x)$.
- $\left(\dfrac{f}{g}\right)(x) = \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ with the $x$ where $g(x) = 0$ removed.

Example: $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$, $g(x) = x - 4$: $f/g$ has domain $[0, \infty) - \{4\}$.

**Composition (formative only, not assessed in the annual paper):** $(g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x))$. In general $g \circ f \ne f \circ g$: for $f(x) = 2x + 1$, $g(x) = x^2$, $(g \circ f)(2) = 25$ but $(f \circ g)(2) = 9$.

key_terms.definition_md: $D_f \cap D_g$, where both functions are defined.

visual.alt: Table of the four combinations of f of x equal square root of x and g of x equal x minus 4: the sum, difference and product have domain from 0 up, the quotient also excludes 4; at x equal 9 the values are 8, minus 2, 15 and three fifths.
visual.caption: $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ and $g(x) = x - 4$.

visuals.alt: Table for f of x equal square root of x minus 1 and g of x equal x minus 5: the sum and product have domain from 1 up, the quotient also excludes 5; at x equal 10 the product is 15 and the quotient is three fifths.
visuals.caption: $f(x) = \sqrt{x - 1}$, $g(x) = x - 5$.

visuals.alt: Flow diagram of a composition: the input 2 goes through f of x equal 2 x plus 1 to give 5, then through g of x equal x squared to give 25, so g after f at 2 is 25.
visuals.caption: $g \circ f$: apply $f$ first, then $g$.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Cartesian product (1–2 marks):* all pairs, correct order, correct count $pq$.
- *Relation from a rule (2–3 marks):* roster form 1, domain 1, range 1.
- *Is it a function? (1–2 marks):* test every element of the first set for exactly one arrow; quote the failing element.
- *Domain and range (2–3 marks):* excluded values or an interval for the domain; solve $y = f(x)$ for the range.
- *Graph (2–3 marks):* shape, key points, corners and jumps.
- *Algebra of functions (2–3 marks):* expression, common domain, zeros of the divisor removed.

**Common mistakes**
1. Writing $B \times A$ when $A \times B$ is asked, or assuming they are equal.
2. Giving the codomain as the range.
3. Counting relations as $pq$ instead of $2^{pq}$.
4. Leaving out an element of the domain that has no arrow, or putting it in.
5. Forgetting to remove the zeros of $g$ in the domain of $f/g$.
6. $[-0.4] = 0$: the greatest integer not exceeding $-0.4$ is $-1$.
7. Concluding $\dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}$ and $x + 2$ are the same function (their domains differ).
8. Composition and exponential-logarithmic graphs are light topics: composition is formative only.

cards.front_md: When are two ordered pairs $(a, b)$ and $(c, d)$ equal?

cards.back_md: All ordered pairs $(a, b)$ with $a \in A$, $b \in B$.
Not in general: equal only if $A = B$ or one set is empty.

cards.front_md: $n(A \times B)$ in terms of $n(A) = p$ and $n(B) = q$?
What is $A \times B$ if $A$ is empty?

cards.back_md: The set of all points of the coordinate plane.
The set of first entries of its pairs.

cards.front_md: Codomain of a relation from $A$ to $B$?

cards.back_md: The set of second entries that actually occur (a subset of the codomain).

cards.front_md: Number of relations from $A$ to $B$, $n(A) = p$, $n(B) = q$?
Number of non-empty relations from $A$ to $B$?
Four ways to describe a relation?
Picture: an element of $A$ with no arrow. Is it in the domain?
cards.back_md: No; it is not a first entry.
A relation giving every $x \in A$ exactly one image in $B$.

cards.front_md: Two ways a relation fails to be a function?
cards.back_md: An input with two images, or an input with none.

cards.front_md: Number of functions from a $p$-element set to a $q$-element set?

cards.back_md: If some vertical line meets the graph twice, it is not a function of $x$.

cards.front_md: How do you find the range of a real function?
cards.back_md: Solve $y = f(x)$ for $x$; keep the $y$ for which a real $x$ in the domain exists.
Mirror images in $y = x$; $2^x$: range $(0, \infty)$, $\log_2 x$: domain $(0, \infty)$.

cards.front_md: Is $g \circ f = f \circ g$ in general?
cards.back_md: No: for $f(x) = 2x + 1$ and $g(x) = x^2$, the values at $2$ are $25$ and $9$.

questions.stem_md: For two non-empty sets $A$ and $B$, the Cartesian product $A \times B$ is the set of

options.text_md: all ordered pairs $(a, b)$ with $a \in A$ and $b \in B$
all elements that belong to both $A$ and $B$
all unordered pairs $\{a, b\}$ with $a \in A$ and $b \in B$
all ordered pairs $(b, a)$ with $b \in B$ and $a \in A$

questions.solution_md: The first entry of each pair comes from $A$ and the second from $B$, and the order matters. Option (d) describes $B \times A$ and (b) is the intersection.

questions.stem_md: A set $A$ has $4$ elements and a set $B$ has $5$ elements. The Cartesian product $A \times B$ has how many elements?
questions.solution_md: Each of the $4$ elements of $A$ pairs with each of the $5$ elements of $B$: $4 \times 5 = 20$ ordered pairs. Option (d) adds instead of multiplying.

questions.stem_md: Two ordered pairs are equal: $(2x + 1,\ 3y - 4) = (9,\ 11)$. Then $x + y$ is
questions.solution_md: Equal ordered pairs have equal entries in the same positions: $2x + 1 = 9$ gives $x = 4$ and $3y - 4 = 11$ gives $y = 5$, so $x + y = 9$. Forgetting to divide by $2$ or by $3$ leads to $13$ and $11$.

questions.stem_md: Let $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$ and $B = \{2, 4\}$. Which ordered pair is **not** an element of $A \times B$?
questions.solution_md: A pair $(a, b)$ is in $A \times B$ only if $a \in A$ and $b \in B$. In $(2, 3)$ the second entry $3$ is not in $B$.

questions.stem_md: A set $A$ satisfies $n(A \times A) = 49$ and a set $B$ has $5$ elements. Then $n(A \times B)$ equals
questions.solution_md: $n(A)^2 = 49$ gives $n(A) = 7$, so $n(A \times B) = 7 \times 5 = 35$. Option (c) multiplies $49$ by $5$.

questions.stem_md: $A = \{x \in \mathbb{N} : x \le 3\}$ and $B = \{y \in \mathbb{Z} : |y| \le 1\}$. The number of elements of $A \times B$ is
questions.solution_md: $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$ and $B = \{-1, 0, 1\}$ both have $3$ elements, so $n(A \times B) = 3 \times 3 = 9$. Dropping the negative integer from $B$ gives the tempting $6$.

questions.stem_md: $R$ is the relation from $A = \{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}$ to $B = \{-1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$ given by $y = x^2 - 1$. The range of $R$ is
questions.solution_md: The pairs are $(-2, 3), (-1, 0), (0, -1), (1, 0), (2, 3)$. The second entries are $3, 0, -1, 0, 3$, so the range is $\{-1, 0, 3\}$. Option (d) is the codomain and (b) is the domain.

questions.stem_md: The number of different relations from a set $P$ with $2$ elements to a set $Q$ with $3$ elements is
questions.solution_md: $P \times Q$ has $2 \times 3 = 6$ pairs and a relation is any subset of it: $2^6 = 64$. Option (a) is the number of pairs, not of subsets.

questions.stem_md: A relation $R$ from $\{1, 2, 3\}$ to $\{2, 3, 4\}$ is given by $x\,R\,y$ if and only if $x < y$. How many ordered pairs does $R$ contain?
questions.solution_md: $x = 1$ is below $2, 3, 4$ ($3$ pairs); $x = 2$ is below $3, 4$ ($2$ pairs); $x = 3$ is below $4$ ($1$ pair). Total $3 + 2 + 1 = 6$.

questions.stem_md: In a relation $R$ from a set $A$ to a set $B$, the codomain is

options.text_md: the set $B$, whether or not every element of it occurs in $R$
the set of all first entries of pairs in $R$
the set of second entries that actually occur in $R$

questions.solution_md: The domain is the set of first entries and the range is the set of second entries that occur. The codomain is the whole target set $B$.

questions.stem_md: Which of these relations from $\{1, 2, 3\}$ to $\{a, b\}$ is a function?
questions.solution_md: A function gives **every** element of $\{1, 2, 3\}$ exactly one image. (a) leaves $3$ without an image; (b) gives $1$ two images; (d) gives $3$ two images. Only (c) works; two inputs may share an image.

questions.stem_md: The domain of the real function $f(x) = \sqrt{6 - 2x}$ is
questions.solution_md: The square root needs $6 - 2x \ge 0$, so $2x \le 6$ and $x \le 3$. Dividing by $-2$ would reverse an inequality, but here it is only moved across.

questions.stem_md: The real function $f(x) = \dfrac{x + 1}{x^2 - 4}$ has domain
questions.solution_md: The function is undefined where the denominator is zero: $x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2) = 0$ at $x = 2$ and $x = -2$. The numerator vanishing at $x = -1$ causes no problem.

questions.stem_md: Which interval contains exactly the values taken by $f(x) = 4 - 3x^2$ as $x$ runs over all real numbers?
questions.solution_md: Since $x^2 \ge 0$, $3x^2 \ge 0$ and $f(x) = 4 - 3x^2 \le 4$, with the value $4$ reached at $x = 0$. Large $|x|$ makes $f(x)$ as negative as we like. So the range is $(-\infty, 4]$.

questions.stem_md: The range of the real function $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x - 2}$ is
questions.solution_md: For a value $y \ne 0$, solving $\dfrac{1}{x - 2} = y$ gives $x = 2 + \dfrac1y$, which is a legitimate input. The value $0$ is never reached because a fraction with numerator $1$ is never $0$. The excluded value $2$ belongs to the domain, not the range.

questions.stem_md: Here $[x]$ is the greatest integer not exceeding $x$ and $\operatorname{sgn}$ is the signum function. The value of $[-2.3] - \operatorname{sgn}(-4) + [1.8]$ is
questions.solution_md: $[-2.3] = -3$ (the greatest integer not above $-2.3$), $\operatorname{sgn}(-4) = -1$ and $[1.8] = 1$. So the value is $-3 - (-1) + 1 = -1$. Truncating $-2.3$ to $-2$ would give $0$.

questions.stem_md: The lowest point on the graph of $y = |x + 3| - 1$ is
questions.solution_md: $|x + 3|$ is smallest ($0$) when $x + 3 = 0$, that is $x = -3$, and then $y = 0 - 1 = -1$. The graph of $|x|$ has been shifted $3$ units left and $1$ unit down.

questions.stem_md: For $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ and $g(x) = x^2 - 16$, the domain of the quotient function $\dfrac{f}{g}$ is
questions.solution_md: The domain of $f/g$ is the common domain $[0, \infty)$ with the zeros of $g$ removed. $g(x) = 0$ at $x = \pm 4$, and only $x = 4$ lies in $[0, \infty)$. The point $0$ stays, since $g(0) = -16 \ne 0$.

All three cases agree, so the identity holds for every real $x$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Need $16 - x^2 \ge 0$, i.e. $x^2 \le 16$: domain $[-4, 4]$. On it $0 \le 16 - x^2 \le 16$, so $0 \le f(x) \le 4$, and every $y \in [0, 4]$ occurs at $x = \sqrt{16 - y^2}$. Range $[0, 4]$.

**(b)** $x^2 + 1 \ge 1$ is never $0$, so the domain is $\mathbb{R}$. Put $y = \dfrac{1}{x^2 + 1}$: then $x^2 = \dfrac{1 - y}{y}$, which has a real solution exactly when $\dfrac{1 - y}{y} \ge 0$, i.e. $0 < y \le 1$. Range $(0, 1]$.

**(c)** $|x - 2|$ is defined for every real $x$, so the domain is $\mathbb{R}$. Since $|x - 2| \ge 0$, $h(x) \le 5$, with $5$ reached at $x = 2$, and every $y \le 5$ occurs at $x = 2 + (5 - y)$. Range $(-\infty, 5]$.

questions.stem_md:
Let $f(x) = x^2 - 4x$ and $g(x) = \sqrt{x}$.

(a) State the domains of $f$ and $g$.

(b) Find $(f + g)(x)$ and $(fg)(x)$ with their domains.

(c) Find $\dfrac{f}{g}$ and its domain, and simplify the expression.

(d) Find the domain of $\dfrac{g}{f}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $f$ is a polynomial: domain $\mathbb{R}$. $g$ needs $x \ge 0$: domain $[0, \infty)$.

**(b)** On the common domain $[0, \infty)$: $(f + g)(x) = x^2 - 4x + \sqrt{x}$ and $(fg)(x) = (x^2 - 4x)\sqrt{x}$.

**(c)** $\dfrac{f}{g}$ needs $g(x) \ne 0$, and $g(0) = 0$, so the domain is $(0, \infty)$. There, $\dfrac{f}{g}(x) = \dfrac{x(x - 4)}{\sqrt{x}} = \sqrt{x}\,(x - 4)$.

**(d)** $\dfrac{g}{f}$ needs $f(x) \ne 0$ in addition. $f(x) = x(x - 4) = 0$ at $x = 0$ and $x = 4$. Removing both from $[0, \infty)$ leaves $(0, \infty) - \{4\}$.

questions.solution_md: Intersect the domains; remove zeros of the divisor.

questions.stem_md:
$A = \{a, b, c\}$ and $B = \{1, 2\}$.

(a) Find $n(A \times B)$.

(b) How many different relations are there from $A$ to $B$?

(c) How many of these relations are functions from $A$ to $B$?

(d) How many are **not** functions?

(e) How many functions are there from $B$ to $A$?

Give a reason for each answer.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $n(A \times B) = 3 \times 2 = 6$.

**(b)** A relation is any subset of $A \times B$, which has $6$ pairs: $2^6 = 64$ relations.

**(c)** A function gives each of the $3$ elements of $A$ one of $2$ images: $2^3 = 8$ functions.

**(d)** Not functions: $64 - 8 = 56$.

**(e)** Each of the $2$ elements of $B$ chooses one of $3$ images: $3^2 = 9$ functions.

questions.solution_md: Product rule for functions; subsets for relations.

questions.stem_md:
The figure shows the graphs of $f(x) = |x + 1|$ and $g(x) = 3 - x$.

(a) Write $f(x)$ without a modulus sign for $x \ge -1$ and for $x < -1$.

(b) Solve $f(x) = g(x)$ in each of the two cases, and give the point where the graphs meet.

(c) Hence find all $x$ for which $f(x) < g(x)$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** For $x \ge -1$, $f(x) = x + 1$. For $x < -1$, $f(x) = -(x + 1) = -x - 1$.

**(b)** Case $x \ge -1$: $x + 1 = 3 - x$ gives $2x = 2$ and $x = 1$, which satisfies $x \ge -1$. Case $x < -1$: $-x - 1 = 3 - x$ would need $-1$ to equal $3$, which is impossible, so there is no solution there. The graphs meet only at $x = 1$, where $y = 2$: the point $(1, 2)$.

**(c)** For $x \ge -1$: $x + 1 < 3 - x$ gives $x < 1$, so $-1 \le x < 1$. For $x < -1$: $-x - 1 < 3 - x$ becomes $-1 < 3$, true for every such $x$. Together, $f(x) < g(x)$ exactly for $x < 1$.

questions.passage_md: A school coding club in Pune (an imagined club) has four students, Asha, Bilal, Chitra and Dev, and three project themes: Web, App and Game. Each student may sign up for any themes. The sign-ups are the relation $R$ from the set $S$ of students to the set $P$ of themes: Asha chose Web and Game, Bilal chose Web, Chitra chose Game, and Dev chose Web.

children.stem_md: Which statement about R is correct?

options.text_md: R is a function, because Web was chosen by three students
R is a function, because every student signed up for a theme
R is not a function, because Asha appears with two different themes

children.solution_md: A function gives each student exactly one theme. Asha has two, so R fails. An unused theme in the codomain is allowed, and several students may share a theme.

children.stem_md: How many ordered pairs of S × P are not in R?
children.solution_md: $S \times P$ has $4 \times 3 = 12$ pairs and $R$ has $5$ of them, so $12 - 5 = 7$ pairs are not in $R$.

children.stem_md: **(i)** Write the domain and the range of R, and say how many themes of the codomain are not in the range.

answer.model_answer_md: Domain $= \{\text{Asha}, \text{Bilal}, \text{Chitra}, \text{Dev}\}$ (every student appears). Range $= \{\text{Web}, \text{Game}\}$. So $3 - 2 = 1$ theme, App, is not in the range.

children.solution_md: First entries give the domain; second entries the range.

alternatives.stem_md: **(ii)** The club now insists that each student signs up for exactly one theme. How many different sign-up patterns are possible, and how many of them use all three themes?

answer.model_answer_md: Each of the $4$ students has $3$ choices: $3^4 = 81$ patterns. Patterns missing a chosen theme: $2^4 = 16$, for $3$ choices of theme, giving $48$; patterns missing two themes were subtracted twice, so add back $3$. Using all themes: $81 - 48 + 3 = 36$.

alternatives.solution_md: Product rule, then inclusion and exclusion.
